HSBC says every G7 member will need Italian-style primary surpluses to stabilise debt, as Rome borrows more cheaply than Paris ahead of an election-year budget.

In September 1992, Italy was the cautionary tale of European finance. The lira was forced out of the European exchange rate mechanism, the currency slumped, and Rome had to convince investors that it could still pay its bills.

What followed was more than three decades of belt-tightening that Italians still argue about. Year after year, the state collected more in revenue than it spent, before counting the interest on its debt.

Economists call this a primary surplus. Italy has posted one in 28 of the 34 years since 1992, according to International Monetary Fund data.

Now one of the world's largest banks says the rest of the Group of Seven will have to do the same.

"Every member of the G7 will have to follow Italy," Janet Henry, global chief economist at HSBC, said in a note last week titled "Turning Italian?".

Her argument rests on simple arithmetic. When the interest rate a government pays on its debt stays above the growth rate of its economy, debt keeps rising as a share of output, unless the government spends less than it collects before interest.

With borrowing costs high across advanced economies, Henry expects that gap to persist.

A lesson Italy learned the hard way

Henry was careful not to turn Italy into a model pupil.

"Italy is no poster child: the debt stock is still high, but it has run a persistent primary surplus for many years, initially forced by a severe currency and debt crisis in 1992," she said.

The difference, in her view, is that Rome has kept up the effort for decades, while the others have barely started.

"Unlike Italy, none of the others are on track for a prolonged adjustment," Henry said.

Only countries that have felt some pressure from bond markets, such as the United Kingdom, have tried to tackle their deficits over the past year, she added.

Not even the United States escapes the problem. Henry cited an estimate by the director of the Congressional Budget Office, the US fiscal watchdog, that stabilising American debt through growth alone would require nominal growth of 7-8% a year at current rates.

She also warned that the easy exits are closed. Governments cannot slash spending the way Greece and Portugal did after the eurozone crisis, and productivity gains from artificial intelligence may not easily turn into higher tax revenue.

"Difficult political choices lie ahead," she said.

Only one G7 country spends less than it collects

The latest IMF figures show how lonely Italy's position is.

According to the Fund's October Fiscal Monitor, Italy is on course for a primary surplus of 1% of GDP this year, rising to 1.2% in 2027. It is the only G7 economy expected to run one.

France is heading for a primary deficit of 2.9% of GDP this year. Germany, long the eurozone's fiscal disciplinarian, is projected to run a primary deficit of 3.4% as it ramps up spending on defence and infrastructure.

The United States is expected to run a primary deficit of 4.9%, Canada 2.6%, and Japan and the UK about 1.2% each.

How far the others would have to travel is a matter of debate. Writing in the IMF's Finance & Development magazine in March, economist Zsolt Darvas estimated that France and the United States would each need a primary surplus of 1.3% of GDP to stabilise their debt, and the UK 1.8%.

For France, that would mean improving its budget by more than four percentage points of GDP. Darvas noted that Paris has hit the required level only six times in five decades.

Italy, to be clear, still carries the heavier load. The IMF expects its public debt to reach 137.9% of GDP this year, the highest in the eurozone and above Greece's 136%. France stands at 118.5%.

Bond markets have already changed their minds

Investors appear to have reached a similar conclusion to HSBC.

On Monday at 13:26 CET, Italy's 10-year government bond yielded 4.43%, while France's equivalent OAT yielded 4.93%.

That means Rome is borrowing for a decade at half a percentage point less than Paris. On Friday, the gap closed at 50 basis points, the widest in Italy's favour since at least 1999, according to TradingView data.

The reversal has been fast. At the start of 2025, Italy paid 34 basis points more than France. The two lines crossed in September 2025, and the gap has kept widening since.

Italy now also borrows more cheaply than the UK, where the 10-year gilt yields 5.35%, and the United States, where the 10-year Treasury yields 5.12%.

Against Germany, the eurozone's benchmark, the BTP-Bund spread stands at 106 basis points. The spread measures the extra return investors demand to hold Italian rather than German debt. France's equivalent gap is 156 basis points, more than double the 71 basis points it started the year at.

Italy has not been immune to this year's sell-off. Its spread has widened from about 60 basis points in late February, as the war in the Middle East pushed up energy prices, inflation expectations and borrowing costs across Europe.

Claus Vistesen and Melanie Debono, economists at Pantheon Macroeconomics, expect that move to unwind.

"We think the BTP-Bund spread will fall next year, more than reversing its widening this year," they said in a note on Thursday. "We look for a BTP-Bund spread of 20bp by mid-2027, from just over 100bp at the moment."

Part of their reasoning is France. They argue that its more serious fiscal problems, along with uncertainty around next year's presidential election, will keep investors turning to Italian bonds.

Even then, cheaper relative borrowing would not make Italy's debt cheap. "Yields will stay high, at just above 3%, keeping the Italian government's debt costs elevated for now," they said.

An election-year budget tests the model

The bigger test for Italy may come from Rome itself.

Giorgia Meloni's government approved its 2027 budget on 28 October, a package worth about €26 billion that is now going through Parliament.

Much of it is tax relief.

For 2027 only, the 33% income tax band would be extended to earnings of up to €55,000, from €50,000.

Young private-sector workers born after 1997 and earning up to €28,000 would pay a flat 1% tax on pay rises of up to €2,500. Raises from renewed labour contracts would be taxed at a flat 5% for workers earning up to €33,000.

The self-employed would be able to stay in the flat-tax regime with turnover of up to €100,000, up from €85,000.

Car tax would be permanently scrapped for one insured car of up to 80 kilowatts per owner, and mothers of two or more children earning up to €40,000 would receive a tax-free €100 a month.

To pay for part of it, banks and insurers face a three-point rise in corporate income tax for two years, energy companies a higher regional business tax, and the tax on financial transactions would double to 0.8%.

Italy's Court of Auditors, which oversees public spending, told lawmakers on 9 November that many of the tax breaks expire at the end of 2027 and that about 70% of the funding will not be repeated, leaving the bill to the next Parliament.

The government's own fiscal plan, published in October, sees the deficit at 2.9% of GDP this year, rising to 3.4% in 2027 once extra defence and energy spending allowed under EU rules is included.

Debt is projected to edge up to 138.5% of GDP next year.

A vote too close to call

The budget lands as Italy heads towards a general election due by autumn 2027, with growing talk in Rome of an earlier vote in the spring.

The latest SWG poll for broadcaster La7, published on 9 November, put the centre-left opposition on 44.9% and Meloni's centre-right coalition on 44%, a gap within the margin of error.

Meloni's Brothers of Italy remained the largest single party on 28.9%, while 29% of respondents did not state a preference.

Pantheon's base case is that the governing coalition survives the vote, which it sees as a further reason for the spread to stay tight through 2027.

In 1992, Italy had no choice but to tighten its belt. Thirty-four years later, the rest of the G7 is being told to do the same, just as Italy is being tempted to loosen its own.

Tokyo's announcement came hours after South Korea said it had deployed fighter jets and conducted tactical manoeuvres after several Russian military aircraft entered its air defence zone.

Japan said on Tuesday it scrambled fighter jets after suspected Russian aircraft violated its airspace, prompting Tokyo to lodge a protest with Moscow in a further deterioration of relations between the two countries.

Russia and Japan have a decades-old dispute over the status of a string of islands in the Pacific Ocean, but their relations have further soured in recent weeks following the arrest of a Japanese journalist on spying allegations and the seizure of assets belonging to a Japanese tobacco firm.

The two "suspected Russian" planes entered Japan's airspace close to Okinoshima, in the southwestern area of Fukuoka, shortly after 4:00 am on Tuesday (2000 CET on Monday), top government spokesman Minoru Kihara said.

Japanese jets sent warnings to the aircraft, which breached the country's airspace for around three minutes each.

"The violation of our national airspace by Russian aircraft is not only a grave infringement of our country's sovereignty, but also a threat to our security and is completely unacceptable," Kihara said.

"We lodged a very stern protest with Russia through diplomatic channels and strongly demanded measures to prevent any recurrence."

Kihara said the aircraft travelled through the Tsushima Strait and went between Yonaguni island and Taiwan before heading to the Pacific.

Tokyo's announcement came hours after South Korea said it had deployed fighter jets and conducted tactical manoeuvres after several Russian military aircraft entered its air defence zone.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) in Seoul said an unspecified number of Russian aircraft entered and later exited the Korea Air Defence Identification Zone (KADIZ) over the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan, in the early hours of Tuesday.

An air defence identification zone is not sovereign airspace but a buffer area in which countries identify approaching aircraft for security purposes.

Military aircraft are generally expected to notify the relevant country before entering its air defence zone, although such notification is not legally required.

Seoul said the Russian aircraft did not violate South Korean airspace.

Takaichi and Putin talks?

Japan lodged a "very serious protest" with Moscow in 2024 after a Russian patrol plane entered its airspace three times. That was the first confirmed incursion since 2019.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Russian President Vladimir Putin are both due at an Asia-Pacific summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen this week.

Multiple Japanese media outlets reported that Tokyo had asked for a meeting between Takaichi and Putin at APEC, while the Kremlin said on Monday it hadn't ruled out the possibility of talks.

Tensions between the two nations are high after Japan demanded earlier this month the immediate release of Japan Tobacco's assets in Russia, which were seized in the latest move against a foreign company's Russian operations under rules that Moscow casts as retribution for international sanctions.

In October, Russia's FSB security service arrested Japanese journalist Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper on allegations of "conducting espionage activities on Russian territory".

Russia's foreign ministry has also accused Tokyo of systematically using journalists for espionage operations inside the country.

Japan has denied the allegations.

From Xylella to avocados, Salento is testing a new type of agriculture. But the spread of the bacterium worries Europe, and the tropical turn raises a key challenge: water availability.

Hass, Bacon and Fuerte: in Salento the new stars of the countryside have exotic names. Between Calimera and Vernole, in the province of Lecce, these avocado varieties are now an increasingly tangible presence, to the point that in mid November the harvest swung into full gear. They are no longer just an agricultural curiosity but a conversion gamble for Apulian farms seeking an alternative after the mass destruction of olive trees caused by Xylella fastidiosa.

That gamble, however, also has a downside. Avocado needs a lot of water precisely during the hottest summers, in a region already grappling with drought and aquifers under pressure.

The transformation is visible at the Tommasi farm, where the first plants were put in the ground in 2017. Almost ten years on, each tree produces between 70 and 100 fruits, for an estimated yield of around 10 quintals per hectare. Last April another 700 trees were planted.

And while Salento changes its crops, Xylella continues to pose a threat to European agriculture, turning a crisis that began in Apulia into a problem for the entire Mediterranean.

Xylella, a threat that no longer concerns only Apulia

The story of Salento’s avocado in fact starts with that of the lost olive trees. In October 2013 Xylella fastidiosa was detected for the first time in the European Union, in Apulia. It is a bacterium that colonises the xylem, the tissue through which water and nutrients circulate, progressively compromising the way the plant functions. In olive trees it can cause rapid desiccation and, in the most serious cases, the death of the tree.

Since then the disease has reshaped vast areas of Apulia’s agricultural landscape. And it has not remained confined to Italy: over the years it has also been found in France, Spain and Portugal. The crops affected include not only olive trees but also almond trees, citrus, vines and various ornamental plants.

The scale of the problem is confirmed by scientific research. In the latest update of its host plant database, published in 2025, the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) recorded 727 plant species in which the presence of Xylella has been reported. For 463 of these there is stronger scientific evidence, based on specific detection criteria. This does not mean that all are equally vulnerable or that every subspecies of the bacterium can infect them: its ability to cause disease depends on the combination of bacterial variety, host plant and environmental conditions.

In 2026 new warning signs also emerged in Italy. In Calabria, in the territory of Taurianova in the province of Reggio Calabria, seven olive trees tested positive for the pauca subspecies. It is the first outbreak in the region. In Basilicata, meanwhile, the multiplex subspecies was detected on an almond tree in the Matera area. Emergency plant health measures and eradication operations have been put in place in both territories.

The spread of the bacterium makes surveillance an issue that goes beyond regional and national borders. For Europe, protecting agricultural production also means preventing a local outbreak from becoming a problem for entire supply chains.

The potential bill for European agriculture

How much could an uncontrolled spread of Xylella cost? An assessment published in November 2025 by the Joint Research Centre of the European Commission (JRC), together with EFSA, confirmed the bacterium as one of the main plant health threats for the Union.

In a large-scale spread scenario, annual production losses could reach 7.1 billion euro, with more than 540,000 jobs at risk. This is a simulation of potential impact, not a tally of damage that has already occurred.

The figure shows clearly why Xylella is not just an Apulian issue. Olive growing, almond production, citrus and winegrowing are important economic activities in several European countries. Loss of output would also have consequences for processing companies, distribution and all the businesses linked to agricultural value chains.

The European Union has therefore introduced specific rules to combat the bacterium. Xylella is classified as a quarantine pest organism and Implementing Regulation 2020/1201 lays down obligations for surveillance, delimitation of outbreaks and removal of infected plants.

When the bacterium is found in a new territory, the general rule is eradication: infected areas and buffer zones are established, with checks and plant removals as set out in the legislation. Where the disease is already widely established and elimination is no longer considered realistic, as in some parts of Apulia, containment measures are applied. Annual surveys are also carried out in the member states, and European co-financing is available for surveillance and control activities.

Prevention, however, does not bring back the lost olive trees. And this is where the search for new crops comes in.

Avocado, mango and papaya: the new face of southern farmland

For farmers who have lost a large part of their olive heritage, diversifying can mean avoiding abandoning their land and building new sources of income.

According to calculations by the Department of Soil, Plant and Food Sciences at the University of Bari, in Apulian areas affected by Xylella there are 23,885 hectares of olive groves potentially suitable for avocado cultivation. Land in Apulia devoted to tropical crops is already thought to total 4,000 hectares.

This is not just a business choice. Rising temperatures are changing the conditions in which traditional crops grow and creating opportunities for species that just a few decades ago would have been difficult to cultivate in these areas. Avocado, mango and papaya are among the clearest examples.

Climate data confirm the speed of change. According to Coldiretti Puglia’s processing of ERA5-Land data from Copernicus, in the first ten months of 2026 the Italian temperature anomaly reached +2.11 degrees compared with the 1991-2020 average. It is the highest value in the national data series for the January-October period.

But higher temperatures do not automatically mean better farming conditions. A crop may find a thermally favourable environment and still be unsuitable because of its water use, soil quality or vulnerability to extreme events.

Avocado: thrives in the heat but is thirsty

This is the main critical point of Salento’s conversion. Avocado is a subtropical species that requires a significant water supply, especially in the summer months. Olive trees, by contrast, are Mediterranean plants able to withstand prolonged periods of drought, thanks to physiological adaptations to the environmental conditions of the region.

The root system of the avocado is concentrated mainly in the upper layers of the soil, making the plant particularly dependent on available moisture. Agronomic estimates indicate water use that can reach 136-220 litres per day for an adult tree in summer, with lower values in spring.

The fruit’s water footprint is also significant. According to calculations by the Water Footprint Network by Mekonnen and Hoekstra, producing one kilogram of avocado requires on average 1,981 litres of water, taking into account rainwater, water used for irrigation and the water needed to dilute pollutants.

Naturally, not all litres have the same weight: rainwater and water drawn from aquifers and watercourses are different resources. It is therefore important to distinguish between the overall water footprint and actual irrigation water use.

For Salento, however, the problem remains concrete. Avocado is also sensitive to water salinity and poorly draining soils. These are particularly problematic characteristics in an area where underground reserves are under pressure and seawater intrusion is a documented risk.

A reprieve from drought is not enough

Apulia formally ended on 30 June 2026 its state of emergency over water shortages, after abundant rainfall in the previous winter and spring. But the end of the emergency does not equate to solving the problem.

Data from the ANBI Observatory updated at the beginning of October showed that the four artificial reservoirs in the Capitanata area contained 98.12 million cubic metres of water, less than 30 per cent of their total authorised capacity of 331.9 million.

In Salento, moreover, agricultural supply depends to a significant extent on underground resources. Hydrogeological surveys by Ispra have long documented falling aquifer levels and seawater intrusion, which can compromise the quality of available water.

The risk is that the expansion of crops with high water requirements will increase pressure on wells, fuelling competition between agricultural activities and household use. This difficulty is not confined to Apulia: water management has become one of the central issues for the future of Mediterranean agriculture, which is increasingly exposed to dry spells and irregular rainfall.

A new agriculture, but not at any price

Salento’s avocado shows that agricultural conversion can open up opportunities even in territories hit by a devastating plant health crisis. But it is not a universal solution. The trees take years to come into production, they require specific investments and they remain exposed to winter cold snaps, which can damage plantations.

The challenge, therefore, is to choose crops not only on the basis of new temperatures but also of actual water availability, soil quality and the ability to withstand extreme weather events.

Russian strikes hit two major bridges in Kyiv late on Monday, part of an overnight attack that damaged critical infrastructure and disrupted heating and water in parts of the capital, the city's mayor said.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned of an attack by Russia in the coming days even as negotiators representing Kyiv as well as Europe and the United States held talks on future negotiations with Russia aimed at finding a path to end the war.

"Tonight, overnight, and throughout tomorrow, please pay attention to missile danger alerts," he said.

"And they there, in Russia, must know that for every one of their evils there will be our just response," he added.

"Preliminarily, hits to the North and South bridges in the capital," Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko posted on Telegram just before midnight local time (2300 CET), shortly after the Ukrainian air force warned of incoming missiles.

"As a result of the enemy attack, critical infrastructure systems have been damaged," he said in a later post, adding heating and water supplies in some districts were affected.

Ukraine also launched drones at Russia's capital region overnight, according to its mayor, and hit a symbolic bridge in the annexed Crimean peninsula, its Russian-installed governor said.

Moscow's mayor Sergey Sobyanin said in the early hours of Tuesday morning that air defences had repelled 20 drones heading towards the capital.

Ukraine for the second day in a row also struck a symbolic bridge that links the annexed Crimean peninsula to Russia, Crimea's Moscow-installed governor, Sergey Aksyonov, said Tuesday.

"At the moment, traffic is suspended," he posted on Telegram.

Missiles from Pyongyang

Zelenskyy also said Monday that Russia was receiving "dozens of missiles per month" from North Korea, calling on European allies to send more weapons to respond "on equal terms" to the threat.

"Russia is unfortunately receiving more ballistic missiles from North Korea. We are talking about dozens of missiles per month," Zelenskyy said. He added that "Europe has missiles that can deliver truly effective strikes" and asked allies to help in "countering Russian global banditry".

North Korea has sent thousands of troops to support Russia's nearly four-year full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to South Korean and Western intelligence agencies.

France, Britain, Germany, Poland, Italy and European Union negotiators have been chosen to represent the continent at future talks with Russia.

Zelenskyy said the five countries, the EU and a NATO representative had been involved in the latest talks with the US envoys.

"The conversation was not easy, but there is a result," the Ukrainian leader added, without giving details.

Kushner confirmed the talks, which he said included national security advisers from the European nations, and insisted that "progress" was being made to end the war.

He said much of the focus of talks had been on ways to "facilitate direct engagement" between Ukraine and Russia.

"While much of the public discussion focuses on the differences between the parties, we continue to see positive and constructive ideas emerging through serious discussions away from the public spotlight," Kushner said in a post on X.

A new study ranks different types of extreme weather by how many lives they claimed in 2025.

As world leaders debate what to do about climate change at COP31 in Türkiye, they may want to take onboard new research into the economic and human costs of extreme weather.

There was one climate disaster a day on average in 2025 – and both rich and poor countries were badly affected.

The report, which does not account for the current ‘godzilla’ El Niño, shows how fossil fuel-driven warming is making extreme weather more deadly and more economically damaging.

Spain, France, Italy and Romania were in the top 20 most affected countries worldwide in 2025, with further extreme weather this year showing it was not a one-off event.

Almost a million lives lost to extreme weather in the last 30 years

In 2025, 367 extreme weather events were recorded worldwide, according to the Climate Risk Index (CRI) 2027. They caused nearly 35,000 deaths (it’s very likely the actual number is much higher than this as heat-related deaths are severely

underreported in poorer countries), affected more than 100 million people, and caused direct economic losses of more than US$158 billion (€143 billion).

Looking back over the last 30 years, 900,000 people lost their lives to extreme weather events and they resulted in direct economic losses totaling more than US$4.7 trillion (€4.2 trillion) – almost equivalent to Germany’s current GDP.

Between 1996 and now, the period the study looked at, rich countries, like Spain, France and Italy, have become much more vulnerable to deadly weather. The report’s authors say these countries should take the CRI results as a warning of the risks they face of frequent events, or rare but extraordinary extreme events: “The human losses and economic costs of climate-related extreme weather events will continue to rise unless there is a sizeable shift in mitigation ambition and financial support.”

In 2025, Jamaica, Sri Lanka and Spain were the most affected countries, followed by Thailand, the Philippines and Pakistan.

Why was Spain the third worst country for extreme weather in 2025?

Spain was hit by seven extreme weather events in 2025, with hundreds more that were devastating for local communities but not classed as extreme.

Spain’s deadliest event was a heatwave which spanned April to September and saw temperatures hit 46°C. It claimed 3,900 lives officially but is likely to have contributed to many more deaths. At the time, 2025 was Spain’s hottest summer ever, on average 2.1°C warmer than the 1991-2020 average, but it has now been surpassed by 2026.

Heatwaves kill people because high temperatures, especially when combined with humidity, impair the body’s ability to cool itself. This increases the risks of cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, kidney failure, diabetes complications and mental health impacts. Health impacts are highly unequal – older people, children and those living in inadequate housing are more likely to die.

2025 was Spain’s worst wildfire season in three decades

A particularly dry spring in western Spain, followed by the heatwave wiping out any remaining moisture in dense, dry vegetation, led to 2025 being Spain’s worst wildfire season in three decades.

The European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS) estimated that 382,607 hectares burned – about 1.5 times the size of Luxembourg.

Fires raged across Galicia, Asturias, Castilla y León and Extremadura. These regions, with the exception of Extremadura, are among the most depopulated in the country. Depopulation impacts forest upkeep. Traditional practices like extensive livestock grazing, which once naturally cleaned up the forest during the winter and spring, have largely disappeared. Fire brigades across the affected autonomous communities have repeatedly warned about the lack of forest management and limited resources.

The costliest event was Storm Alice, which caused US$100 million (€91m) in economic losses and affected more than 1,000 people. Alice triggered a weather event called a cold drop (Depresión Aislada en Niveles Altos), with rains leading to flooding.

Why heatwaves are such bad news for people – and the economy

Heatwaves were by far the deadliest type of extreme weather events in 2025, accounting for almost 70 per cent of all deaths.

Italy was the worst hit, with 6,710 deaths during a summer that reached 45.7°C, followed by 3,893 in Spain. In Germany, a heatwave reaching 38.3°C in July and August was the only extreme weather event registered in 2025. Nevertheless, it led to more than 2,400 fatalities.

Heatwaves are very bad news for the economy. In Germany, each day above 30°C is estimated to cause €124 million in economic losses, while globally output per hour generally declines by around USD$1.3 (€1.20) per worker for each additional degree between 30°C and 35°C.

Rising temperatures lower productivity and increase accidents and sick leave. Physically demanding jobs like construction are worst affected – with countries like Italy often having to ban outdoor work during the hottest hours of the day. Less output lowers tax revenues, while heat-related healthcare costs increase.

For informal workers, like fruit pickers or market traders, their earnings can fall by around 40 per cent during heatwaves, potentially pushing them into debt or having to take their children out of school.

Heatwaves can also disrupt infrastructure, as seen in Europe this year when nuclear power plants in France, Romania and Hungary had to shut down because there wasn’t enough water to keep them cool. Low river levels can also disrupt transport and increase costs for affected companies.

What are the solutions to reduce extreme weather?

Negotiators at COP31 could turn things around for all of us, with experts saying they must agree to transition away from fossil fuels. According to the UN, fossil fuels – coal, oil and gas – are by far the largest contributor to global climate change, accounting for around 68 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions and nearly 90 per cent of all carbon dioxide emissions. Extreme weather has become more extreme, frequent and deadly as emissions have risen.

Europe has been making good strides in the transition away from fossil fuels and to clean, renewable energy sources like wind and solar power. Many homeowners have got onboard by installing heat pumps in their homes. Policymakers need to direct more money away from fossil fuels and towards renewables.

When it comes to reducing deaths during heatwaves, cities that focus on reducing the urban heat island effect perform better. More trees and green space and less polluting vehicles are two of the keys to cooler cities. Milan, one of Europe’s most polluted cities, recently won a global prize for its plans to plant four million new trees and shrubs, helping to purify its smog-cloaked streets.

Ordinary citizens are also key in pressuring governments to take the climate crisis seriously and take real action. The glaring exclusion of High Representative Kaja Kallas from the Ukraine-Russia peace talks has raised uncomfortable questions about the relevance of her job. Defiant but isolated, Kallas stands by her words.

Since taking on the job as the European Union's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas has dealt with her fair share of setbacks, rebuffs and snubs.

But this one particularly stung.

Last week, Kallas flew to Dublin to attend an informal summit of leaders and make a forceful pitch to become the special European envoy for the ongoing negotiations to end Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

She framed her argument to leaders as self-evident: you chose me for this.

"In June 2024, there was a decision by the leaders (on) who is representing (the EU) when it comes to security and foreign policy. And it was the discussion that in these five years there is going to be a negotiation with the Russians," she said, referring to the division of top jobs at the start of the legislature.

"If the leaders want to change that agreement, of course, they may, because it is the leaders' decision, but I think we should focus our energy actually on the substance."

But leaders were unmoved and dismissed her pitch outright. According to people familiar with the closed-door discussions, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni argued that Kallas lacked the institutional weight and discouraged her candidacy.

The summit concluded with an expanded joint European team for the negotiations with a grand total of seven representatives. None of them was Kallas.

Adding insult to injury, the EU seat is shared by the European Council and the European Commission, with senior officials from the cabinets of presidents António Costa and Ursula von der Leyen, respectively. The European External Action Service (EEAS), the institution that Kallas oversees, is out of the picture.

Asked about her absence, neither Costa nor von der Leyen spoke in her favour.

Snubbed and pushed aside, Kallas now stares down a political reality in which she, the High Representative, whom the treaties task with conducting the EU's common foreign and security policy, is excluded from the most consequential diplomatic process the continent has lived through since the end of the Cold War.

It is a contradiction so glaring and profound that it challenges the very essence of her job.

Some in Brussels believe what happened in Dublin is the natural consequence of the missteps and gaffes that have made Kallas an increasingly divisive – and increasingly isolated – figure in the big-power city.

Kallas has ruffled feathers by going off script on sensitive matters, such as China and Israel, and putting forward initiatives with little or no prior consultation with capitals, including a defence expert group whose launch was cancelled last minute in September after pushback from Italy, France and others.

The displeasure has fuelled calls to reform. Germany, for instance, has proposed to place Kallas under von der Leyen's supervision, mimicking the top-down hierarchy in national governments between a prime minister and a foreign minister.

A senior diplomat pointed out that Kallas spent this year opposing direct talks with Russia, only to then pitch herself as the special envoy to deal with Moscow.

"If she actually talked to people and consulted with them, she would have known where the dynamics would lead to," the diplomat said. "Now, events have overtaken her."

"On the merits she is not wrong," they admitted. "Nothing will come of these talks anyway. There's no way Russia will engage constructively."

A second diplomat was equally critical and said Kallas had been very "clumsy" in her intervention in Dublin, where she declared "Russians don't want me" as envoy.

This diplomat believes that Kallas still retains the way of working she had when she was Estonian prime minister. Back then, her outspoken, hawkish views made her a political star in Europe. In her current role, they can easily backfire.

"It was not the right approach. She put herself in a difficult position. She still has in mind the fact that she was prime minister, and forgets that her role is simply to coordinate the positions of the foreign affairs ministers," the diplomat said.

"Her job is to find the lowest common denominator among member states."

Doomed to fail

The High Representative's pitch was doomed to fail for reasons that go beyond personalities, management style and political background.

Russia's war on Ukraine has become the be-all, end-all subject on the political agenda. Defence, security, trade, energy, finance, technology, sanctions and accession are all at stake in Ukraine. Billions have been provided in budget, military and humanitarian aid. How the war ends is set to define Europe for generations to come.

This has compelled leaders to be extraordinarily involved in the conflict, with countless visits to Kyiv and high-profile meetings. The decision by the leaders of France and the UK to launch the Coalition of the Willing best encapsulates the personal commitment.

But their commitment has come to the detriment of their foreign ministers and eaten away at their portfolios. More often than not, foreign ministers find themselves bickering and haggling without making decisions, which are ultimately made by leaders.

In fact, for the peace talks, leaders have relied on their national security advisors, who are part of their tight-knit cabinet. Even US President Donald Trump has left the task on two hand-picked envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, rather than on Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who, compared to Witkoff and Kushner, is harder on Russia.

Kallas, whose title is equivalent to Rubio, has suffered a similar fate.

Earlier this year, Kallas promoted a list of maximalist demands that Europeans should press Russia to fulfil as part of the negotiations.

Though the document was confidential, the High Representative quoted it so many times, including in Dublin last week, that she effectively made it public. While foreign ministers debated the document at length, leaders never acknowledged it and proceeded with their deliberations unconcerned by its existence.

"The reality is that no foreign minister has an obvious leading role here. Not because foreign ministers are irrelevant, but because the decisions at stake go far beyond traditional foreign policy," a third diplomat said.

"This is, quite literally, a matter for heads of state and government. They are the ones who can ensure political coherence across different areas and ultimately take responsibility for the commitments involved."

A fourth diplomat put it more succinctly, saying Europe should focus its energy on establishing a "consistent, unified position" for the negotiations rather than getting caught up in "unproductive discussions" of names.

Admittedly, the demise of the High Representative is a story that has been written many times in the past and never proven correct – or at least not its entirety.

The prevailing opinion blames the byzantine architecture of the EU treaties, which envisions a high-ranking figure bound by the principle of unanimity and deprived of enforcement powers, as the root cause of the problem.

Still, most diplomats agree that the Estonian's way of working is an aggravating factor. The lack of backing from the Commission, where she serves as vice president, and member states, whose views she is meant to represent, leaves her vulnerable to attacks. When backlash erupts, she is left to fend for herself.

Outside Brussels, however, Kallas remains popular and her no-nonsense takes on Russia are frequently praised and go viral online. The fact that the Kremlin openly detests her is used by her defenders to argue she is doing a great job.

Asked by Euronews if she regretted pitching herself as special envoy so forcefully, Kallas remained defiant.

"I stand by my words and I'm ready to do this job," she said, calling on leaders to uphold the EU treaties the same way they uphold the rule of law.

But she added: "It's also some kind of relief that we don't take about who any more.'

French car maker Renault announced on Monday plans to create 2,000 jobs by 2028, mostly production roles, while cutting 1,000 mainly administrative staff as it seeks to hold off tough Chinese competition.

French carmaker Renault announced on Monday plans to create 2,000 jobs by 2028, mostly in production, while cutting 1,000, mainly administrative, posts as it seeks to fend off tough competition from China.

The carmaker presented unions with its France Industrie FutuREady project, which aims to transform its industrial activities to respond to the growing challenge posed by Chinese carmakers to European vehicle manufacturers.

The reorganisation will involve the creation of 2,000 new jobs over two years, mainly "blue-collar" positions, Thierry Charvet, head of quality, manufacturing and supply chain, said during a call with journalists.

Renault has around 15,000 industrial jobs in France.

The plan will see 1,650 operators and production workers hired at its plants, along with 250 employees in indirect functions and 100 young graduates.

Renault also announced 1,000 voluntary departures among "white-collar" staff in indirect and administrative functions, under a scheme that still has to be negotiated with the unions.

The CFDT trade union criticised the pace of the planned changes as a "forced march schedule".

Certain jobs deemed strategic will be protected, including those in battery engineering, electronics and software, electric powertrains and industrial maintenance.

The company announced in September that it would invest €600 million ($660m) in Spain by 2030 to produce five new models.

Europe's car industry faces weak demand, excess production capacity and intensifying competition from Chinese manufacturers.

A massive European genome bank could pave the way for medicines tailored to each patient's DNA, faster diagnosis of rare diseases and new ways of prevention. Here's how it works.

Could a medicine one day be designed on the basis of the genetic characteristics of the person who is going to take it?

Could doctors know in advance which patients are more likely to respond to a treatment or to develop side effects?

And could the genetic causes of diseases that are currently hard to diagnose be identified more easily?

Personalised medicine is no longer just a distant scientific vision. Some of its applications are already used in clinical practice, while wider deployment requires much more knowledge of the human genome.

The Genome of Europe programme is one of the largest European population genomics projects. In total, 49 partners from 27 European countries are working together to create a shared reference base of at least 100,000 human genomes, which will reflect the genetic diversity of European populations.

The programme has a budget of €45 million, of which €20 million come from the European Commission through the Digital Europe programme. The project officially started in the autumn of 2024 and is scheduled to run for 3.5 years.

Cyprus is taking part in this effort through the Centre of Excellence for Biobanking and Biomedical Research biobank.cy at the University of Cyprus. Its contribution includes sequencing the whole genome of at least 310 Cypriot volunteers, feeding into the European reference base.

Why Europe needs a genetic map

Human DNA is, to a large extent, shared by all of us. However, small genetic differences are important for understanding inheritance, predisposition to certain diseases and, in specific cases, how people respond to medicines.

These differences are not distributed in the same way across all populations. This means that a genetic database built mainly from specific population groups may not adequately capture the genetic diversity of others.

Genome of Europe aims to close this gap by creating a representative European dataset that can be used as a reference point for future research.

"Populations, such as that of Cyprus, have their own specific characteristics," explained Katerina Strati, an associate professor in the biological sciences department at the University of Cyprus.

She told Euronews that understanding the genome at the local level is essential, because the relevant information cannot simply be inferred from research in other populations.

For scientists, a reference genome acts as a yardstick. It allows them to examine the genetic variants they identify in a person and to assess how common or rare they are in the population to which that person belongs.

Cyprus maps its own DNA

Mapping the Cypriot genome in its current form began in 2019, Strati explains. The aim is to create a genetic reference background for the country’s population, which will support medical research and molecular diagnosis.

Under the Cypriot Human Genome Project (CYPROME), more than 1,000 exomes from Cypriot volunteers have already been analysed. The exome is the part of the genome that includes the protein-coding regions of genes. Its analysis differs from sequencing the whole genome, which examines a much larger section of DNA.

Apostolos Malatras, a senior bioinformatician at the Centre of Excellence biobank.cy, explained that creating a reference genome allows researchers to compare genetic findings against a common background.

We will help make it much easier to design medicines and, of course, to use them: if a person has difficulty using a specific medicine, we will create a specialised medicine for that person

Today, biobank.cy holds more than 123,000 biological samples, involves 12,257 volunteers and is active in 14 research programmes, according to the figures published on its website.

The samples do not correspond one to one to genomes or participants. A volunteer can provide more than one sample, and DNA sequencing is a separate process.

Studies carried out at the Cyprus Biobank focus on hereditary kidney diseases, heart conditions and other illnesses. Its research programmes also include efforts to develop preclinical models for rare kidney diseases such as Alport syndrome.

Mariel Voutounou, a project manager at the Centre of Excellence, described the search for a treatment as a long and demanding marathon.

"When a doctor or scientist is interested in starting research into a condition, we say that they are starting a time-consuming marathon. And that is because it takes a great deal of time and effort to collect all these data and samples," Voutounou said. "Someone who has a whole biobank and this wealth of information in their toolbox, we say that their starting line is 10 kilometres ahead of everyone else."

Who protects patients’ DNA?

DNA contains highly sensitive information, not only about a person’s health but also about their biological relatives. How is it ensured that the genetic data of thousands of volunteers will not be used without their knowledge or consent?

The Cyprus Biobank operates with the approval of the National Bioethics Committee of Cyprus and in accordance with the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). As Malatras explains, biobank.cy applies multiple layers of technical and organisational security, with restricted access to personal data.

Dr Georgia Charalambidou, who is responsible for ethical, legal and social issues (ELSI) and education at the centre, explained that protection begins even before the first sample is collected.

"When a volunteer, an individual, comes here to the centre, the first thing we do is to provide them with sufficient information," Charalambidou said. "We try to make sure that they have understood it. We give them time to process it, to ask us questions and of course a consent form is always signed, in which all their rights are recorded."

Participation remains voluntary even after signing. "We always explain that they can withdraw their consent at any time, without any impact," Charalambidou stressed, clarifying that in the case of patients this decision does not affect their treatment or their relationship with their treating doctor.

The centre has also carried out a survey involving around 569 Cypriots, examining their views on genetic tests and taking part in genetic research.

According to Charalambidou, most participants were positive towards genetic research but want transparency and information about how their data are used. At the same time, they are interested in being able to receive results from the studies in which they take part.

"They want to know how we handle their data, what results exist. They also want to get something back," she said.

She noted that those who had been in contact with patients with diagnosed conditions were more positive about receiving genetic results back from specialist doctors. This finding, she added, highlights the need for better public information on genetic research.

Data work together without travelling

How can scientists in different countries use genetic data without putting their security at risk?

This is what the European Genomic Data Infrastructure (GDI) programme aims to ensure. It works alongside Genome of Europe, creating infrastructure for the secure interconnection of genetic data.

As Malatras explained, researchers will be able to carry out analyses on the systems where the data are stored, without the files themselves needing to be transferred from country to country.

This cooperation is particularly important for rare diseases, as it allows genetic findings from different populations to be compared.

Precision medicine is already used in some treatments, especially in oncology. However, the development of medicines tailored to the genetic characteristics of each patient remains a long-term prospect.

This is also the ambition behind the European collaboration: that the knowledge now being gathered from the DNA of thousands of volunteers will help deliver better diagnoses, more effective prevention and treatments tailored to patients’ needs.

American users of several major banking apps and online portals reported outages on Monday, according to the monitoring site Downdetector.com, with one institution ruling out a cyberattack as the cause.

Among those affected by the outages were Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase and the popular money transfer app Zelle.

Downdetector said outage reports peaked at around 2pm Eastern Standard Time (8pm CET) before subsiding.

JPMorgan Chase said in a statement posted on X that it "has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems", adding that "there is no evidence this is cyber-related".

"It is taking longer than usual to service some customers," the statement continued, with the banking giant vowing to restore service by the end of the day on Monday.

"Where we were party to a transaction involving other banks, those banks may have been impacted, but this is not a systemic issue," JPMorgan Chase added.

The outage initially sparked concerns that it could be cyber-related.

Last month, cryptocurrency platform Binance was the victim of a hack involving $6.3 billion (€5.72bn) in stolen funds, the largest such incident ever in crypto.

More recently, French bank Credit Mutuel Arkea was the target of a cyberattack, losing around €100 million.

Was this related to the Microsoft and air traffic disruptions last week?

No. While the disruptions took place just days apart, government officials and company leaders have said they were unrelated.

The major outage at Microsoft on Thursday, which lasted for hours, severely affected services including Outlook, Teams and the AI assistant Copilot. It was due to a technical issue that arose during an upgrade. The tech giant has said there is "no indication" that the disruptions were caused by malicious activity, such as a cyberattack, or by the actions of artificial intelligence agents.

Another outage that affected the nation's air traffic control system on Friday, grounding all US flights for several hours and disrupting domestic air travel over the weekend, was caused by a router that malfunctioned and overwhelmed the ageing air traffic control system.

Sursele au avertizat că Statele Unite sunt incredibil de vulnerabile la un atac cu arme neconvenționale. Bombele murdare – care ambalează materiale radioactive într-o bombă convențională – sunt relativ ușor de asamblat. Iranul nu ar trebui neapărat să introducă ilegal în țară oameni antrenați, ci ar trebui doar să convingă o persoană care locuiește deja în Statele Unite să comită atacul, scrie CNN.

Serviciile de informații americane au interceptat comunicații iraniene conform cărora Teheranul ar fi ascuns materiale pentru fabricarea bombelor în Statele Unite, potrivit uneia dintre surse. Oficialii sunt împărțiți în ceea ce privește credibilitatea acestor informații, dar, în general, cred că ar fi foarte ușor și chiar probabil ca Iranul să fi pre-poziționat deja materiale nucleare sau agenți chimici care ar putea fi aplicați pe o bombă convențională.

”Oricât de poroasă a fost granița noastră timp de aproape zece ani, ar fi fost extrem de ușor să introducă agenți în interiorul țării” care ar putea achiziționa și plasa componente ale bombei, a declarat una dintre sursele apropiate informațiilor. Mulți oficiali din domeniul securității naționale presupun că materialele nucleare pre-poziționate se află deja în SUA de ani, dacă nu de decenii, a spus o altă sursă. Cu alte cuvinte, capacitatea Iranului de a lansa acest tip de atac nu a crescut, a spus o altă sursă. Ceea ce s-a schimbat este motivația iraniană.

Sursă: CNN
